title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: when the structure goes down, and when either word will do

questions.prompt: Your book ends a chain of sentences with a joke: "The more I study, the more I know. The more I know, the more I forget. The more I forget, ……… I know. So, why study?" Which completion makes the joke work?

options.text: the more
the fewer
the less
the least

questions.explanation: The joke needs the chain to turn back on itself, so the last link must go down while the others went up — and knowledge is uncountable, so its downward comparative is less. That reversal is also the reason your book calls the structure parallel change rather than parallel increase: the same shape can rise or fall. the fewer would be right for a countable noun, such as the fewer books I read, but you cannot count knowledge. Repeating the more keeps the chain climbing and destroys the joke. And a superlative cannot appear here at all, since each half compares itself only with the half before it.

questions.prompt: Your book prints the question "Would you like to have some coffee?" in its list of some, and "Would you like to have any coffee?" in its list of any. Which explanation is right?

options.text: One of the two is a misprint and should be corrected.
Both are correct: some offers, any asks neutrally.
Both are correct and mean exactly the same thing.
Only the one with any is correct, since it is a question.

questions.explanation: The two sentences are both English and they differ in what the speaker expects: some turns the question into an offer that anticipates yes, while any leaves the answer genuinely open. Calling one of them a misprint misses the very point the book is making by printing them together. Saying they mean the same empties the choice of any purpose, and if that were so the book would not need two lists. And ruling out some because the sentence is a question would also rule out the book's own Did you see some tall men, which is an interrogative with some and appears on the same page.

questions.prompt: A pupil must write to the National Association of Nurses for information about the profession. She does not know who will read her letter. Which opening should she use, and how should she punctuate it?

options.text: To whom it may concern,
Dear Sir or Madam.
To Whom It May Concern:
Dear Association,

questions.explanation: The formula is capitalised on every word and followed by a colon, exactly as the model letter in your book prints it, and it is used precisely when the writer has no name to address. Written in lower case with a comma it loses both the capitals and the punctuation the form requires. Dear Sir or Madam is a real alternative, but it must end in a comma, not a full stop, so that version is wrong on its punctuation rather than on its wording. And addressing an organisation as though it were a person is not done: Dear followed by a name works for people, never for an association.

questions.prompt: Read this note about a school library. "The library has fewer readers every year, and the staff have less time for each of them." Why does the sentence use fewer once and less once?

options.text: Because readers can be counted and time cannot.
Because fewer is more formal than less.
Because the first half is about people and the second about things.
Because fewer must always come before less in a sentence.

questions.explanation: fewer is the downward comparative of a countable noun and less that of an uncountable one, so readers takes fewer and time takes less. Formality plays no part: the two words are not two registers of one idea but the answers to two different questions about the noun. Nor is the split between people and things, since chairs are things and still take fewer while patience belongs to people and takes less. And no rule of order governs them; either can open a sentence, and the noun beside each is what decides.

questions.prompt: Which sentence would a careful reader refuse to write today about the music industry, without adding a date?

options.text: A single is a record with one song on each side.
Compilation albums can compete with individual singles.
Only ten singles sell more than ten thousand copies a week.
Radio stations sometimes play a song before it is released.

questions.explanation: The figure of ten singles above ten thousand copies belongs to one week of January 2002, and quoting it in the present tense claims that it is still true, which nothing in the text supports. The definition of a single is not a measurement at all — your book prints it as a glossary entry, and a definition does not expire. That compilations compete with singles and that radio plays songs before release are general mechanisms rather than counts, so they survive without a year attached. The rule is simple: date the numbers, and only the numbers need dating.

questions.prompt: A pupil hesitates between two structures for the same idea. Which sentence uses the parallel-change structure correctly?

options.text: The library becomes more and more crowded, the exams get closer.
More the exams get closer, more the library becomes crowded.
The closer the exams get, the more crowded the library becomes.
The closer the exams get, more crowded becomes the library.

questions.explanation: The structure needs the in front of both comparatives, a subject and a verb in each half, and a comma between them, which is what the third sentence provides. The first sentence describes one thing changing steadily with more and more and then simply places another clause beside it, so the two changes are never tied together. The second drops both instances of the and copies a word order English does not use for this pattern. And the fourth begins correctly but then loses the on the second comparative, which breaks exactly the link the structure exists to make.
